context: The legend at the bottom defines the complexity parameters. The number of elements is n. For bucket sort, k is the number of buckets. For counting sort, m is the range of values. For radix sort, k is the maximum number of digits and b is the base. Read k in the context of its row because it measures different quantities in different algorithms.

The four properties on the right are stability (whether equal elements keep their original relative order), in-place operation (whether elements are rearranged without an auxiliary array comparable in size to the input, with the recursion stack still counted in space complexity), adaptivity (whether existing order can reduce the work), and use of comparisons (whether the algorithm compares element values or uses key distributions or digit counts).
description: Braces on the left group the nine algorithms into scan-based sorts, divide-and-conquer sorts, and linear sorts. The main table lists best-case, average, and worst-case time, but only worst-case space. Its remaining four columns show stability, in-place operation, adaptivity, and use of comparisons.

The figure uses pale green for “good,” pale blue for “fair,” and grayish purple for “poor.” The table expresses each background color as a rating in parentheses. All three time entries for radix sort are O(nk), but the figure rates the best and average cases as good and the worst case as poor. The table retains those ratings. They are not absolute judgments for every practical setting.

Bubble sort's O(n) best-case time and adaptivity assume the optimized version that stops after a pass with no swaps. Quicksort's O(log n) worst-case space assumes the tail-recursion or stack-depth optimization that recurses only on the shorter subarray and loops over the longer one. Ordinary recursion without this optimization takes O(n) stack space in the worst case.

Bucket sort is marked stable on the assumption that the sort within each bucket is stable. Its O(n+k) best-case and average time require the total cost of sorting the buckets to remain linear. For example, the data may be uniform and the number of buckets may grow with n so each bucket has a constant expected size. Uniform data alone is insufficient if there are too few buckets. If all elements land in one bucket and it uses a quadratic sort, the worst-case time degrades to O(n²).

Counting sort's O(n+m) time depends on the value range m. Radix sort's O(nk) time assumes a fixed base b. If b also varies, each counting sort pass takes O(n+b) time, giving O(k(n+b)) for k passes. All three linear sorts have requirements on the type and range of data. The O(n) category label is not an unconditional time bound.

frames.explanation: Sorting algorithms involve trade-offs. None in the figure is rated good on every measure. In practice, consider data size, expected degree of order, value range, memory limits, and stability requirements together.
frames.title: Comparison of sorting algorithms

summary: Compare nine common sorting algorithms by time complexity, space complexity, and four properties. Choose an algorithm based on the implementation and the characteristics of the data.
